jobs.tts: Good morning, and welcome aboard. I'll be your guide from the capital to the redwoods: across the floodplain, over the hills into Napa or Sonoma, and down to the Russian River at Gurn-vill. I'll chime in when there's something worth knowing, and keep quiet when there isn't. Tap the screen any time to see what I'm saying, or to skip me. We're starting beside the Sacramento River, the reason this city exists at all. Sacramento grew up on the waterfront, because the river was the highway to the coast. Old Sacramento, the riverside historic district, still has its nineteenth-century brick buildings, the most notable dating from just after a disastrous fire in 1852. Before the levees went up, the area flooded so often that the city raised its streets a whole storey, which is why there are still tunnels and buried storefronts under Old Sac. That golden lift bridge you may have glimpsed is the Tower Bridge, opened in 1935, with towers 160 feet tall. When it was dedicated, a thousand homing pigeons were released to carry the news across California. It was painted gold in 2002 after a public vote, which some locals still grumble about. Right, let's head west.

One name will follow us all day: Sam Brannan. He was a printer and a Mormon elder who sailed a shipload of Latter-day Saint emigrants round Cape Horn to California in 1846, bringing a printing press and a complete flour mill with him. He founded the California Star, San Francisco's first newspaper, and he's considered the first person to publicise the Gold Rush. His stores supplied the rush, and the profits made him California's first millionaire. He bought land everywhere, including a hot-springs valley at the far end of the Napa Valley that we may pass through later: he named it Calistoga. It didn't end well. He helped form San Francisco's first vigilance committee, which got him disfellowshipped from his church. His wife divorced him, and he had to sell much of his real estate to pay her half. Brannan died poor and fairly obscure. In Old Sacramento, the Sam Brannan House, built in 1853, still stands.

You've crossed into Yo-lo County and the city of West Sacramento. Its story begins with a widow. In 1849, James McDowell was shot dead in a bar argument he'd apparently started, leaving his wife Margaret with three daughters and 600 acres. She hired a surveyor, divided the land into forty-one blocks, and sold lots in a new settlement she called the Town of Washington. It became a rest stop for travellers struggling through the marshes towards Sacramento, and a busy fishing and farming centre, shipping salmon, sturgeon and crayfish as far as San Francisco. Washington was later renamed Broderick, and together with Bryte and West Sacramento was known as East Yo-lo, until the three finally incorporated as one city in 1987. Today the big industry is the Port of West Sacramento, which opened to ocean-going ships in 1963 at the end of a 43-mile deep-water channel dredged up from Suh-soon Bay. It's an inland port that ships out bulk farm products, rice especially.

Look out at the flat land on both sides. You're on the Yo-lo Causeway, a three-mile viaduct across the Yo-lo Bypass, and this is one of the cleverest pieces of flood control in America. Rather than building ever-higher walls around Sacramento, engineers gave the river somewhere else to go. Upstream, at a concrete spillway called the Fremont Weir, when the Sacramento River rises past a set height the excess simply pours over the top and into this basin. A second set of gates just north of West Sacramento can be opened by hand. In a big flood the bypass can carry several times the flow of the river itself, a shallow inland sea about forty miles long and three miles wide, draining south into the Delta. The causeway you're on stays above it. The idea came from bitter experience. Severe floods in 1862 and 1878 drowned the valley, and Congress approved the Sacramento River Flood Control Project in 1911. The bypass was laid out by the Army Corps of Engineers in the early 1930s. In dry months most of it is farmland, about three-quarters privately owned. Much of the rest is the Yo-lo Bypass Wildlife Area, where rice fields are flooded after harvest, and thousands of ducks and shorebirds settle in plain view of Interstate 80. So if you see water and birds out there, that's not a mistake. That's the plan working.

Before any causeway, crossing this basin in the wet season meant a ferry, or a long detour south through Stockton. The first vehicle to make it across each summer set the line of the seasonal Tule Jake Road. The first causeway opened in 1916, a two-lane timber and concrete trestle, celebrated with a three-day party. In 1928 it was folded into the Lincoln Highway, the first road across America, and later carried Highway 40. Today's twin structures date from 1962. Traffic reporters call them the long bridge and the short bridge. They're officially named for two Highway Patrol officers killed near here in 1978. And underneath you right now, at least in summer, live bats. Roughly a quarter of a million Mexican free-tailed bats migrate to the Yo-lo Causeway every June. They roost in the expansion joints between the concrete segments and feed on insects from the wetlands. It's one of the largest bat colonies in California, and the local foundation runs bat-watching tours at dusk.

Coming up is Davis, a town that began as a railroad stop and became one of the most important agricultural universities on earth. The depot opened in 1868 and was named Davisville after Jerome C. Davis, a prominent local farmer. In 1907 the post office got tired of the extra syllables and shortened it to Davis. In 1905 the state legislature passed the University Farm Bill, and Governor George Par-dee chose Davis from about fifty candidate sites. Berkeley's agriculture dean, Eugene Hill-gard, had admitted that Berkeley's foggy coastal climate was terrible for farming. The University Farm opened to students in 1908 and grew into UC Davis. Its veterinary school is the largest in the United States. Davis is also famously flat, which helped make it a haven for cyclists. It's called the bicycling capital of America, and it's home to the United States Bicycling Hall of Fame. A couple more Davis oddities: students built a cluster of fibreglass geodesic domes, inspired by Buckminster Fuller, back in 1972, and they're still lived in. And Muir Commons, finished in 1991, is known as the first newly built cohousing community in the United States.

Before the farms, the freeway and the university, this western edge of the Sacramento Valley was home to the Pat-win, the southern branch of the Win-toon peoples, who have lived in this part of California since roughly the year 500. The Pat-win lived in settled villages, fishing, hunting and gathering, and acorns were central to life: across the plains and foothills, groves of oaks were a harvest. The southern Pat-win lived between what is now Suh-soon, Vacka-vill and Pew-tah Creek, and as Spanish and later settlers pushed in, they were broken into small groups whose names survive on today's map. The Oo-loo-lah-toss lived at Vacka-vill, around a village on Ulatis Creek downtown. The La-bye-toss lived along Pew-tah Creek, the Ma-lah-kuss in Lagoon Valley, the Toe-lay-nuss in the upper Suh-soon Valley, and the Suh-soon-ess on the Suh-soon Marsh, which carries their name. One of the most famous Pat-win was a leader called Sem Yay-toe, better known as Chief Solano, a diplomat and a friend and ally of the Mexican general Vuh-lay-oh. Then came the Gold Rush. Settlers took the oak groves and water. Smallpox and measles swept through. Many Pat-win were forced into unpaid labour on ranches and in mines, a practice historians describe as another kind of slavery. By the late 1850s the population had collapsed to a fraction of what it had been, and by the 1920s no Pat-win remained along Pew-tah Creek. But the story doesn't end there. Pat-win people today belong to three federally recognised tribes, including the Yo-cha Deh-heh Win-toon Nation, and the language, listed as at risk in 1997, is being taught to a new generation. When Pat-win remains were found during construction of a concert hall at UC Davis, the university built a Native American contemplative garden in its arboretum. And near Fairfield, a hillside park that opened in 2024 carries a Pat-win name: Pat-wee-no Wort-la Ko-doy Dee-hee, which means Southern Rock Home of the Pat-win People. It's managed by a land trust in partnership with the Yo-cha Deh-heh.

Dixon, coming up, is a town that literally picked itself up and moved. During the Gold Rush, a settlement called Silvey-vill grew up here as a halfway stop for miners heading between the coast and the Sacramento gold fields. When the railroad arrived in 1868, it missed Silvey-vill by a few miles. So in 1871 the townspeople relocated, buildings and all, to be next to the tracks. The Methodist church on North Jefferson Street is one of the buildings from that move. The new town was supposed to be Dicksville, after Thomas Dickson, who donated ten acres for the depot. But in 1872 the first rail shipment of goods from San Francisco arrived addressed to Dixon, and everyone just went with it. Dixon has a few claims to fame. The Dixon May Fair, which started as a May Day celebration in 1885, is billed as California's oldest fair. A local pumpkin patch has repeatedly held the Guinness record for the largest corn maze, one of them sixty acres. And near where Highway 113 meets the interstate stands a hundred-foot-tall sign for the old Milk Farm Restaurant, put up in 1963 and still there, long after the restaurant.

This is a geology story, and it starts with a question: why is the Sacramento Valley so astonishingly flat? The answer is that you're driving across the top of an enormous filled-in basin. During the age of the dinosaurs, between about 150 and 65 million years ago, this whole valley was a seaway. To the east, where the Sierra Nevada stands now, ran a chain of volcanoes. To the west, an ocean plate was diving beneath North America, and the rocks scraped off it piled up into a ridge that acted like a dam. Between them lay a deep basin, and the volcanoes eroded into it, shedding mud and sand down underwater canyons into deep-sea fans. Geologists call the result the Great Valley Sequence, and in places it's around 40,000 feet thick, over seven miles. Here's the remarkable part: the volcanic cover of the ancient Sierra has largely been stripped off and used to fill this valley. Most of those ancient sea-floor rocks are now buried beneath younger sediment, but they come to the surface along the valley's western edge, in the hills ahead of you. And the rocks that formed that ancient dam to the west are the Franciscan rocks of the Coast Ranges, which we'll meet later today. Right under the freeway, the geological maps from the Macrostrat database show what came last: alluvial fan deposits, sand and gravel spread by creeks coming out of the hills, and near the river, natural levee deposits, the low ridges that rivers build when they overflow their banks. Near Vacka-vill the maps also show the Tuh-hay-muh Formation, a few million years old, with a layer of volcanic ash called the Pew-tah Tuff. So this flat farmland is the latest layer on a seven-mile stack of history.

Vacka-vill is named after Juan Manuel Vacka, one of two men from New Mexico who came to California in 1841 with the Workman-Rowland Party. Vacka and his partner, Juan Felipe Pen-ya, were granted Rancho Los Poo-toss in 1843: over 44,000 acres, taking in all of present-day Vacka-vill and Lagoon Valley and stretching almost to Davis. The name comes from Pew-tah Creek, then called the Rio de los Poo-toss. It was General Vuh-lay-oh who'd recommended the area to them. Pen-ya's adobe home, built in 1842, is the oldest standing building in the area, now in Pen-ya Adobe Park just south-west of town. Then came the sale that started a feud. In 1850 Vacka sold land to a man named William McDaniel, on condition that a square mile would become a town called Vacka-vill. McDaniel's partner, a Benicia lawyer, acted as interpreter, since Vacka couldn't read or write English. Vacka later said he believed he'd signed away just one square mile, not nine, and he took out a notice in the Benicia newspaper warning everyone not to buy land from McDaniel. Pen-ya was furious too, and the deal soured relations between the two old partners. Vacka-vill grew rich on fruit, with many Japanese and Chinese workers in the orchards and packing companies. And a more recent claim to fame: in August 2022, a truck crash on Interstate 80 here splattered over 150,000 tomatoes across the eastbound lanes, and made international news.

Near the junction with Interstate 505 is the Nut Tree, now a shopping centre, once a California legend. It opened on the 3rd of July 1921 as a little roadside fruit stand on the Lincoln Highway, run by Helen and Ed Power. It was named after a black walnut tree that grew from a nut picked up on a trail in Arizona by a pioneer girl, Sallie Fox, before she arrived in Vacka-vill in 1859. By its second year the stand was serving around 950 cars a day, and it kept growing as the old highway became Interstate 80: a restaurant with a floor-to-ceiling glass aviary, a bakery, a toy shop, its own little railway out to its own airport. Ed Power hired Charles Eames to design the furniture. The restaurant is credited as an early pioneer of California cuisine, built around fresh fruit and vegetables. Reagan, Nixon and Bing Crosby all stopped by, and in 1983 the Nut Tree catered a state lunch for Queen Elizabeth the Second. The original closed in 1996.

The ridge rising to the west is the Vacka Mountains, the easternmost range of California's Coast Ranges, and the wall between the Sacramento Valley and everything we'll see this afternoon. Its east face rises abruptly, a thousand feet or more above the foothills. The highest point, Mount Vacka, is 2,818 feet, the top of Solano County, and the backbone is a long, level crest called the Blue Ridge. Because they're the farthest range from the ocean, the Vacas sit in a rain shadow. They get far less rain than the My-uh-kah-muss Mountains further west, which is one reason the Napa and Sonoma side looks so much greener. The ridgetops are chaparral: chamise, manzanita and buckbrush. Almost all the rain falls in winter, so by late summer and autumn, fire danger here is particularly high. In August 2020, the Hennessy Fire burned through this area and destroyed farms and homes in Vacka-vill. We'll hear more about that complex as we cross the hills.

Keep an eye on the sky to the east and south. If you see something enormous and grey lumbering overhead, it's probably from Travis Air Force Base, a few miles east of Fairfield. Travis calls itself the Gateway to the Pacific, and it handles more cargo and passengers than any other military air terminal in the United States. Its wing flies giant C-5 Galaxies, C-17s and KC-46 tankers, and it's the biggest employer in Solano County. It began in 1942 as the Fairfield-Suh-soon Army Air Base, ferrying aircraft and supplies to the Pacific during the Second World War. After the war it became a Strategic Air Command base, home to B-29s, B-36s and eventually B-52s. The name comes from a disaster. In August 1950, a B-29 carrying a Mark 4 nuclear bomb, without its nuclear core, crashed just after take-off. The fire set off the bomb's conventional high explosives, killing Brigadier General Robert Travis and eighteen others. The base was renamed in his honour the following year.

Fairfield is the home of the Jelly Belly jelly bean, and the story runs from Germany to the White House. Gustav Gay-lits started a sweet business in Illinois in 1869, and the family became big in candy corn. His son Herman moved west and eventually settled the company in Oakland in 1924. In the 1960s they started making a small, intensely flavoured mini jelly bean. Ronald Reagan, who'd given up smoking and taken to sweets instead, first tried them in 1969 and was hooked. As governor in 1973, he wrote to the company that they could hardly start a meeting without passing round the jar. In 1976, a candy distributor named David Klein worked with the family to create a bean with natural flavouring. He came up with the name Jelly Belly, a tribute to the blues musician Lead Belly, and the idea of selling flavours separately rather than as a mix. The first eight were Very Cherry, Tangerine, Lemon, Green Apple, Grape, Licorice, Root Beer and Cream Soda. The company is still headquartered here in Fairfield, though since 2023 it's owned by the Ferrara Candy Company.

Fairfield and the next little place, Cordelia, were both named by one man, a clipper ship captain called Robert H. Waterman. He'd bought into Rancho Suh-soon, a Mexican land grant originally given in 1842 to Chief Solano, which Solano couldn't hold onto and sold to General Vuh-lay-oh, who sold it on. Waterman laid out a town in 1856 and named it after his old home of Fairfield, Connecticut. Two years later he entered it in the race to be county seat and won the title away from Benicia, helped by his offer of sixteen acres of free land for county buildings. Fairfield has been Solano's county seat ever since. Earlier, in 1853, he'd founded a settlement he called Bridgeport. When the Post Office asked for a more distinctive name, he renamed it after his wife: Cordelia. One more local curiosity: in the hills here stood a company town called Cement, founded in 1902 to quarry limestone and make Portland cement. At its peak it had more people than Fairfield, Vacka-vill and Suh-soon City combined, with a three-storey hotel, hospital and baseball diamond. When the limestone ran out it was sold off in 1927. Its biggest concrete ruin, known locally as The Castle, is visible from Interstate 80 in Fairfield.

Just north of Cordelia, in the Suh-soon Valley, stands the Rockville Stone Chapel, built in 1856 by volunteers from local stone, cut from the nearby hills. It's a volcanic ash rock that's soft and easy to cut when quarried but hardens after it's exposed to air. The land was donated by Landy Alford, who'd come west in 1846 in the same wagon train as the ill-fated Donner Party; his son-in-law later helped rescue the survivors. The chapel soon became a casualty of national politics. The congregation split over slavery, and at the Christmas Eve service of 1863 the northern supporters walked out. The southern-leaning members who stayed put a plaque on the building reading M.D. Church South, which is still there. The chapel decayed for decades, was donated to the county in 1929, restored by the Works Progress Administration in 1940, and is still in use today.

To the south lies the Suh-soon Marsh, described as the largest brackish-water marsh on the west coast of the United States: over a hundred thousand acres of tidal marsh, bays and sloughs, where fresh water from the Sacramento and San Joaquin rivers meets the salt of San Francisco Bay. It's named after the Suh-soon-ess, a Pat-win group who lived here. Geologically, it's made of the mountains: sediment worn off the Sierra Nevada and the Vacka Mountains, carried down by rivers and dropped here over thousands of years, with peat soils from the rotting remains of marsh plants. From the Gold Rush until about 1880, market hunters shot waterfowl here to supply San Francisco's markets with fresh birds and feathers. From the 1880s farmers built levees and tried to farm it, until the soil turned too salty even for cattle. Then the big state and federal water projects upstream changed the flow and made the marsh saltier still, and landowners went to the legislature to protect it. Today it's home to river otters, native fish and pelicans.

If you've noticed a railway line running alongside the freeway, it has a sneaky claim to fame. Everyone knows the transcontinental railroad was completed with a golden spike in May 1869. What's less known is that it ended at Sacramento, short of the Pacific. Getting trains on to San Francisco Bay was a separate race. The tracks beside you were built by the California Pacific Railroad, incorporated in 1865 to link Vuh-lay-oh, on the bay, with Sacramento. Its main line from Vuh-lay-oh to Washington, today's West Sacramento, was finished in November 1868, six months before the golden spike. From January 1869 you could take a ferry from San Francisco to Vuh-lay-oh and the train from there. Towns like Davis and Dixon grew around its depots. It even had a branch up the Napa Valley to Calistoga. That made it a valuable shortcut, and the mighty Central Pacific wanted it. When the California Pacific rejected an offer, Central Pacific threatened to build a parallel line, bought up a majority of its stock, and took control. It then built a cut-off across the Suh-soon Marsh to Benicia, which took two years because the marsh was so soft it needed tons of crushed rock. From 1879 whole trains were carried across the Car-keen-ess Strait on a giant ferry. And the line's still busy. Amtrak's Capitol Corridor trains follow the original California Pacific route from Sacramento to Suh-soon-Fairfield, and the California Zephyr and Coast Starlight roll through Dixon without stopping.

The road you're on has been many roads. In 1913 the Lincoln Highway was dedicated: the brainchild of an Indiana entrepreneur, Carl Fisher, and one of the first highways in America designed for cars, running from Times Square in New York to Lincoln Park in San Francisco. At first its backers declined to shift it onto the new Yo-lo Causeway. But in 1928, after the Car-keen-ess Bridge opened, the Lincoln Highway was rerouted over the Yo-lo Causeway and through Davis, Dixon, Vacka-vill and Fairfield, roughly where you are now. When the federal numbered highways arrived, this became U.S. Highway 40. Roadside businesses like the Nut Tree fruit stand grew up on it. In the 1950s and 60s it was rebuilt as Interstate 80, which became the main coast-to-coast route from New York to San Francisco, and old Highway 40 was eventually cut back so far that it now ends in Utah. Even the interstate has moved around. Around Sacramento, I-80 has been realigned several times, and the original route through downtown is now a business loop. And it's still changing: the toll express lanes between Red Top Road in Fairfield and Leisure Town Road in Vacka-vill only opened in December 2025.

You're now on Highway 12 through Jameson Canyon, the gap in the hills between Solano County and Napa. This stretch has history in its bones: in 1928 it became part of the realigned Lincoln Highway, the first road across America. The rocks change here too. The geological maps from the Macrostrat database show the road threading past outcrops of Markley Sandstone, a white to light-grey quartz-and-mica sandstone from the Eocene, around 40 to 50 million years old. Further west come marine sandstones of the San Pablo Group from the late Miocene, including the Cierbo Sandstone, which locally contains shell beds. In other words, these hills are made of old sea floors and beaches, folded and lifted up. And you'll start seeing the volcanic rock that dominates the rest of today: the Sonoma Volcanics, lava flows of andesite and basalt erupted in the late Miocene and Pliocene, between about eleven and three million years ago. Over the ridge, the wine country begins.

Welcome to Napa County, and the Napa Valley. In 1981 this became the second American Viticultural Area in the country, a legally defined wine region, and it's now one of the most famous wine regions in the world, with more than 450 wineries. Here's the layout. The valley floor rises gently north-west, from sea level here near the bay to 362 feet at Calistoga, at the foot of Mount Saint Huh-lee-nuh. On your left as you head north will be the My-uh-kah-muss Mountains, and on your right, the Vacka Mountains we saw from the freeway. Two roads run up the valley: Highway 29 on the west side, and the quieter Silverado Trail on the east. The name Napa is older than any of it. It's of Native American origin, and the most plausible explanation is that it comes from the Pat-win word napo, meaning house. For a while in the 1850s it was even spelled with two p's: Nappa. The local wine story has three acts. A boom in the late 1800s, when the valley had over 140 wineries. A collapse, as a vine pest called phylloxera, then Prohibition, then the Depression knocked it flat. And a revival from the 1960s, crowned in 1976 when Napa wines beat the French at a blind tasting in Paris. I'll tell you those stories as we go.

Somewhere just west of here, beneath the vineyards and marshes between American Canyon and Napa, lies the epicentre of the biggest Bay Area earthquake in a quarter-century. At 3:20 in the morning on the 24th of August 2014, a magnitude 6.0 earthquake struck, centred south of Napa and north-west of American Canyon, on or near the West Napa Fault. It was the largest in the Bay Area since the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake. The shaking lasted ten to twenty seconds. One person was killed and about 200 injured, and damage was estimated between 362 million and a billion dollars. In downtown Napa, historic buildings that had been retrofitted were still badly damaged: the old courthouse, the post office, churches and the Goodman Library. The West Napa Fault is about 35 miles long and was only discovered in 1976, by a groundwater driller from Sebastopol. In 2023 new data showed it's nine miles longer than previously thought. It's part of the broad San Andreas system of plate-boundary faults, which here is about fifty miles wide. And an experimental earthquake warning system alerted seismologists several seconds before the damaging waves arrived.

The city of Napa, off to the east, began as a river town. The Napa River is tidal here, and the town grew at its head of navigation, the furthest point boats could reach. A ship called the Susana made the first recorded trip up the river in 1842, and by 1850 the steamer Dolphin was carrying passengers. Nathan Coombs, who'd arrived in the valley in 1845, laid out the town in 1847 and 1848 on land he'd bought from Nicolás Higuera, holder of the Mexican land grant called Rancho Entre Napa. By the mid-1850s, Napa's Main Street could have a hundred saddle horses tied up on an ordinary afternoon. John Patchett opened the county's first commercial winery in 1859, selling wine for two dollars a gallon. There's a darker chapter. When the first recorded expedition entered the valley in 1823, most of the people here were Native Americans. Tensions with American settlers broke into war in 1850, and soldiers hunted down and massacred those they could find, driving the survivors north toward Clear Lake. By 1870 only a few Native labourers and servants remained. In 1880 the Napa Valley Opera House opened downtown, with Gilbert and Sullivan's HMS Pinafore. Jack London read there in 1905. It closed in 1914, sat empty for decades, and reopened in 2003 with, fittingly, HMS Pinafore again.

For most of its history, the city of Napa was where wine-country tourists drove through, not where they stopped. That changed after a 300-million-dollar flood management project around the turn of this century widened the river and raised the bridges, and developers moved in. The flagship was Coe-pee-uh, the American Center for Wine, Food and the Arts, planned and largely funded by Robert and Margrit Mon-dah-vee and named after the Roman goddess of plenty. It opened in November 2001, just two months after the September 11th attacks, with galleries, theatres, a three-and-a-half-acre kitchen garden and a restaurant called Julia's Kitchen, backed by Julia Child. Visitors never came in the numbers expected, and Coe-pee-uh closed in 2008, its Julia Child cookware sent to the Smithsonian. The Culinary Institute of America bought part of the site and opened a campus there in 2016, beside the Oxbow Public Market. Across the river, on the east side, stands one of the oldest buildings in the valley: the adobe of Cayetano Hwah-ress, a soldier under General Vuh-lay-oh, who was granted Rancho Too-loo-kye in 1841. The name comes from Tuluka, a Pat-win village. His first adobe, built in 1840, still stands and has been used as a restaurant.

You may spot the carriages of the Napa Valley Wine Train, which runs from Napa to Saint Huh-lee-nuh alongside Highway 29. It rides the route of a much older line. Sam Brannan, the Gold Rush millionaire, founded the Napa Valley Railroad in 1864 to carry tourists from the Vuh-lay-oh ferry boats to his hot-springs resort at Calistoga, reaching it in 1868. Southern Pacific later took it over, and passenger service ended in 1929. When Southern Pacific moved to abandon the line in the 1980s, local entrepreneurs bought it for 2.5 million dollars to run a tourist train. Plenty of locals hated the idea, arguing the valley already had too many visitors. They persuaded the state utilities commission to demand a full environmental review, but in 1990 the California Supreme Court ruled, four to three, that the review wasn't needed because the line was already in use. The rails needed around twenty million dollars of repairs before the first wine-and-dine trains could roll. It was an early round in a long fight over how much tourism this valley can take.

Yount-vill is named after George Calvert Yount, and his life reads like a frontier novel. Born in North Carolina in 1794, he fought in the War of 1812, then in 1826 left his wife and children in Missouri to become a fur trapper out of Santa Fe. He reached California in 1831, hunted sea otters off the Channel Islands, and in 1834 went to work as a carpenter for General Vuh-lay-oh in Sonoma. Through Vuh-lay-oh's influence, he received a Mexican land grant in 1836, Rancho Kay-muss, named after a group of Wah-po people, and became the first permanent Euro-American settler in the Napa Valley. He built a blockhouse and a grist mill, and he's credited with planting the valley's first grapevines in 1838. There's a strange story about him, too. Yount said that in the spring of 1847 he had a repeated dream of pioneers struggling in deep snow, and the writer Richard Henry Dana later wrote that Yount's dream helped bring about part of the rescue of the Donner Party. The town was laid out in 1855 as Sebastopol, but a town in Sonoma County had already taken that name, so after Yount died in 1865, it was renamed in his honour. Today almost a third of Yount-vill's residents live at the Veterans Home of California, founded in 1884 and the largest of its kind in the country, with a cemetery holding more than 5,500 veterans and spouses going back to the Spanish-American War.

Yount-vill's other claim to fame is food. The French Laundry, one of America's most famous restaurants, occupies a stone building put up as a saloon in 1896. Then, in 1906, a law banned the sale of alcohol around the Veterans Home, and in 1920 the building became a French steam laundry. Sally Schmitt and her husband Don, then mayor of Yount-vill, opened a restaurant there in 1978 and kept the name, because locals still called the building that. Sally Schmitt was a pioneer of California cuisine, cooking from local, seasonal ingredients. Thomas Keller took over in 1994 and made it a three-Michelin-star destination. In 2020 the restaurant hit the national news when Governor Gavin Newsom attended a dinner there during COVID restrictions, and the name became shorthand for criticism of him. The French connection runs deeper. In 1973 the Champagne house Moët et Shahn-dohn opened Domaine Shahn-dohn here, the first French-owned sparkling wine producer in the Napa Valley, making wine from Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier, the traditional grapes of Champagne.

Let's talk about the ground under all those vines, because in this valley the geology is the product. Start with the shape. The Napa Valley is a long, narrow trough between two ranges, the My-uh-kah-muss on the west and the Vacas on the east. California's great fault system is about fifty miles wide here, a whole family of faults, including the West Napa Fault, slicing north-west through the region and slowly sliding the land past itself. Then the volcanoes. In the late Miocene and Pliocene epochs, between about eleven and three million years ago, this area was volcanic. The result is the Sonoma Volcanics: lava flows, ash and breccia. On the Macrostrat geological maps, the hills around the valley are full of it. There's a dacite breccia under the low hill east of Napa that's interpreted as a resurgent volcano inside an old caldera. Near the Silverado Trail there's the Stags Leap Stock, a granite-like intrusion riddled with quartz veins. Up toward the My-uh-kah-muss you'll find white pumice-rich tuff, ash erupted nearly five million years ago, and glassy rhyolite lava with swirling flow bands, dated to about 5.3 million years. Finally, the gravel. Over the last few hundred thousand years, creeks pouring out of those volcanic and sedimentary hills built fans of gravel and sand across the valley floor. Along Highway 29 the maps show alluvial fan deposits almost all the way to Saint Huh-lee-nuh. In the centre of the valley, the Oakville and Rutherford areas sit on a gravelly rise called the Rutherford Bench, with well-drained soil mixing volcanic deposits and marine sediments from the Franciscan rocks. Oakville's soil is described as gravelly, sandy loam with exceptionally good drainage. So the next time you taste Napa Cabernet, you're partly tasting eroded volcano.

Coming up is Oakville, population about fifty, and some of Napa's most famous Cabernet land. It started in the 1860s as a water stop for Brannan's steam train, named for the dense groves of valley oaks. In 1868 a man called H. W. Crabb bought land near the river and planted a vineyard he named To Kalon, Greek for the beautiful. He experimented with over 400 grape varieties to find what suited the place, and by 1880 had 430 acres of vines. In 1903 the U.S. Department of Agriculture set up an experimental vineyard here, and the Oakville Station is run by UC Davis to this day. In 1965, after a bitter feud with his younger brother Peter over the family's Charles Krug winery, Robert Mon-dah-vee walked out and started his own winery here, the first big new winery in the valley since Prohibition, with part of the old To Kalon land. Its mission-style building, with its great arch and bell tower, opened in 1966. Mon-dah-vee pushed for naming wines by grape variety, Cabernet, Chardonnay, instead of borrowing French place names, and that became the standard across the New World. He even rebranded an unfashionable grape, Sauvignon Blanc, as Fumé Blanc. Forty years after the feud, Robert and Peter made a single barrel of wine together. It sold for 400,000 dollars. Across the highway from Mon-dah-vee is Opus One, his joint venture with Baron Philippe de Rothschild of Château Mouton Rothschild, announced in 1980. A Bordeaux first-growth partnering with a Napa winery gave the valley an air of respectability. Its low, limestone winery was built between 1989 and 1991.

Rutherford is named after Thomas Rutherford, who married one of George Yount's granddaughters. In 1864 Yount gave the couple about a thousand acres, and Rutherford planted it with vines. The great estate here is Ingle-nook, founded in 1879 by Gustave Nee-bowm, a Finnish sea captain who'd made a fortune in the Alaska fur-seal trade and helped promote the Alaska Purchase. He'd wanted to build a winery in France, but his California-born wife disliked long ocean voyages, so Napa it was. Ingle-nook wines won gold medals at the 1889 Paris World's Fair. After decades of corporate ownership, the estate was bought piece by piece by the film director Francis Ford Coppola, starting in 1975 with profits from The Godfather. In 2011 he bought back the Ingle-nook name itself, paying more for the trademark, he said, than he had for the whole estate. Next door is Bowl-you Vineyard, founded in 1900 by Georges de Latour. Legend says his wife Fernande saw the land and exclaimed, quel beau lieu, what a beautiful place. De Latour imported phylloxera-resistant rootstock when the pest was ravaging the valley. And when Prohibition shut down most American wineries in 1920, Bowl-you landed a contract to supply sacramental wine to churches nationwide. Demand for communion wine rose remarkably, and by repeal in 1933 Bowl-you was making over a million gallons a year. In 1938 it hired a winemaker from France, André Chelly-stcheff, who is credited with ushering in modern California winemaking, with small French oak barrels, cold fermentation and frost protection. He mentored a generation, including Robert Mon-dah-vee.

Long before vineyards, the upper Napa Valley was Wah-po country. The Wah-po homelands spread across the Napa Valley, the south shore of Clear Lake, the Alexander Valley and the Russian River valley. Their language belongs to the Yukian family, distantly related to the Yuki people further north. They lived by hunting and gathering, in small, independent groups with no central authority, in homes of branches, leaves and mud. Their baskets were woven so tightly they could hold water. Oaks gave acorns, a staple food, and the hot springs at the head of the valley were a place of healing. There were Wah-po villages near today's Yount-vill, Saint Huh-lee-nuh and Calistoga. The Wah-po name for the Saint Huh-lee-nuh area was Anakotanoma, Bull Snake Village. Calistoga was Nilektsonoma, Chicken Hawk Place. And Mount Saint Huh-lee-nuh, the peak at the head of the valley, was Kanamota, Human Mountain. The name Wah-po is believed to be an Americanised form of the Spanish guapo, which can mean brave. They earned it through stubborn resistance to Mexican rule, holding off military campaigns by General Vuh-lay-oh and his allies until a peace treaty was signed in 1836. What followed was catastrophe. The missions recorded at least 550 Wah-po baptisms. Estimates put the population around 1770 at somewhere between one thousand and 1,650. By the early 1850s it was in the hundreds, by 1880 just fifty, and the 1910 census counted 73. The Wah-po language is now extinct, though a grammar of it was written down. When you see the name Kay-muss on a wine label, that's an echo of a Wah-po group who lived here first.

Welcome to Saint Huh-lee-nuh, the heart of the old Napa wine country. The town was founded in 1854 when two men bought a tract on the west side of Main Street from Maria Ignacia Bale, the widow of an English doctor we'll meet in a minute. It's likely named after the mountain to the north. This is where the valley's wine industry put down roots. Charles Krug started his winery here in 1861; it's often cited as the valley's first. He married Dr. Bale's daughter, and her mother insisted on a prenuptial agreement protecting twenty acres of land north of town, where Krug planted his vines. Much later, in 1943, the Mon-dah-vee family bought the Krug winery for 75,000 dollars, and it's still owned by Peter Mon-dah-vee's family. Beringer, founded in 1876, calls itself the oldest continuously operating winery in the Napa Valley. Its ornate Rhine House was built in 1883 and 84. In 1934, just after Prohibition, Beringer was the first California winery to offer public tours and tastings. In 1939 it lured visitors from San Francisco's world's fair with maps reading All roads lead to Beringer, and invited Hollywood stars like Clark Gable and Carole Lombard. Historians count that as the birth of Napa wine tourism. On Main Street, watch for a vast stone building: Greystone Cellars, built in 1889 as a cooperative winery so small growers could store and age their wine instead of selling it cheap to San Francisco dealers. It was later the Christian Brothers winery and is now the Culinary Institute of America.

On Highway 29 in Saint Huh-lee-nuh is Sutter Home, home of one of the great accidents in wine history. The winery dates to 1874, sat abandoned after Prohibition, and was bought in 1948 by the Trinchero brothers, who scraped by on jug wine. In 1972, Bob Trinchero began making a pale wine from red Zinfandel grapes. Then, making the 1975 vintage, about a thousand gallons of the juice stopped fermenting before all the sugar was used up. He set it aside, tasted it two weeks later, and found it sweet, pink and, in his view, pretty good. They bottled it. By 1987 Sutter Home White Zinfandel was the best-selling premium wine in the United States, and Wine Spectator later credited Trinchero with introducing more Americans to wine than anyone in history. Wine snobs may sniff, but a lot of people's first glass of wine was this one.

By 1880, the Napa Valley was booming. There were 443 vineyards with a thousand or more vines each, most of them around Saint Huh-lee-nuh, and by the end of the century there were more than 140 wineries. Then came three blows in a row. The first was tiny: phylloxera, a louse that attacks grapevine roots. It killed many of the vines throughout the valley. The answer, which Georges de Latour of Bowl-you helped bring in, was rootstock that resisted the pest. The second was Prohibition, enacted in 1920. Many wineries simply shut down. A few survived by making sacramental wine for churches, and growers who kept their vines sold grapes to home winemakers. The third was the Great Depression, which kept the industry down for years. The revival came slowly, through people like André Chelly-stcheff at Bowl-you, Beringer's wine tourism, and a science teacher called Brother Timothy, whose smiling face sold Christian Brothers wine across the country. Then in 1965 Robert Mon-dah-vee built the first big new winery since Prohibition, and the boom returned. And here's the twist: phylloxera came back. In 1983 a new outbreak was found in a vineyard planted on a rootstock called AxR1. Growers used the disaster to replant with better-suited grapes, and by the late 1990s about three-quarters of the affected vineyards had been replanted. Today's worry is a different pest, the glassy-winged sharpshooter, which spreads Pierce's disease. In wine country, the war with bugs never ends.

Watch for the Bale Grist Mill, just off the highway between Saint Huh-lee-nuh and Calistoga, with its 36-foot waterwheel. It's one of only two water-powered mills left west of the Mississippi. It was built in 1846 by Dr. Edward Turner Bale, an English ship's surgeon who landed at Monterey in 1837, became surgeon-in-chief of the Mexican army under General Vuh-lay-oh, and married Vuh-lay-oh's niece. He was granted Rancho Carne Humana, all the land between today's Rutherford and Calistoga. The mill was finished the same year as the Bear Flag Revolt, and there's evidence the rebels met at Bale's mill before they marched on Sonoma. Settlers came from all over the valley to have their corn and wheat ground here, and old-timers swore the slow-turned meal made bread that put city bread to shame. Bale himself tried his luck in the Gold Rush, caught a fever, and died in 1849. Next door is Bothe-Napa Valley State Park, which has the farthest-inland coast redwoods of any California state park. Both parks were threatened with closure in the 2011 budget crisis, and the county parks district stepped in to keep them open.

The approach to Calistoga has some of the valley's most theatrical wineries. Castello dee Amo-roza is a full-scale medieval-style castle, opened in 2007 by the vintner Dario Sattui. It has 107 rooms on eight levels, a moat, a drawbridge, a great hall with frescoes and a torture chamber with an iron maiden he says he bought in Italy for 13,000 dollars. It was built from 8,000 tons of local stone and 850,000 bricks imported from Europe, on land once owned by Dr. Bale. In the 2020 Glass Fire, its farmhouse burned and a whole vintage was lost, but the castle came through unharmed. Nearby, Sterling Vineyards sits on a volcanic hill 300 feet above the valley, reached by an aerial tramway, in a white building inspired by the Greek island of Mykonos, with bells from a London church destroyed in the Second World War. And Shramz-berg, founded in 1862 by a German barber called Jacob Schram, dug its cellars into the hillside in the 1870s. Robert Louis Stevenson visited in 1880 and tasted eighteen wines. Shramz-berg now makes Champagne-method sparkling wine.

Welcome to Calistoga, at the head of the Napa Valley, and the town with the best origin story of the day. It was Sam Brannan again, the Gold Rush millionaire. He visited the hot springs here in 1852, was fascinated, and bought more than 2,000 acres to build a spa to rival the fashionable Saratoga Springs in New York. The story goes that he meant to call it the Saratoga of California, but it came out as the Calistoga of Sarafornia. Whether that's literally true or Brannan just liked the tale, the name stuck. His resort opened in 1862, and his railroad arrived in 1868, bringing San Francisco's rich and famous for the waters. The little depot he built that year still stands. Before all that, this was Nilektsonoma, the Chicken Hawk Place, where the Wah-po had several villages among the oaks and hot springs. The geothermal heat is real. In 1920, a soda fountain owner called Giuseppe Musante was drilling for cold water and hit a hot spring instead. By 1924 he was bottling it, and Calistoga sparkling mineral water became a national brand. And a very modern note: Calistoga now has a hydrogen fuel-cell and battery power plant, built in 2024 and 2025, designed to keep the whole town's lights on for up to 48 hours when the utility cuts power during high fire danger. That's a sign of the times in wine country.

In 1880, a sickly, broke Scottish writer arrived in Calistoga with his new American wife. Robert Louis Stevenson had crossed an ocean and a continent to marry Fanny Vandegrift Osbourne, and friends suggested the mountain air of the upper Napa Valley might help his lungs. They tried the Hot Springs Hotel, but couldn't afford ten dollars a week. So they spent a two-month honeymoon squatting, with Fanny's twelve-year-old son Lloyd, in an abandoned three-storey bunkhouse at a derelict silver mine called Silverado, high on the shoulder of Mount Saint Huh-lee-nuh. They patched the windows with cloth, hauled water by hand and dodged rattlesnakes. The result was a travel memoir, The Silverado Squatters, published in 1883. In it Stevenson used his first telephone, called Napa winemaking an experiment, and noted that some growers labelled their bottles as Spanish to sell them to sceptical Americans. He visited Jacob Schram's winery, and a petrified forest we'll pass shortly. Many of his notes on the scenery later fed into the descriptions in Treasure Island. Today, Robert Louis Stevenson State Park at the summit of Highway 29 protects the site, and a trail leads past the spot where the cabin stood toward the top of the mountain, from where, on a clear day, you can see Mount Shasta, 192 miles away.

Here's the story that put this valley on the world map. In the early 1970s, some California wines were outstanding, but hardly anyone noticed; the market wanted French labels. A British wine merchant in Paris, Steven Spurrier, who mainly sold French wine, organised a tasting with his American colleague Patricia Gallagher to mark America's bicentennial. On the 24th of May 1976, eleven judges, most of them French wine experts, tasted top Chardonnays and Cabernets blind, French against Californian, scoring each out of twenty. Spurrier expected the French to win. They didn't. In both categories, a wine from Napa County came first. The best white was the 1973 Chardonnay from Chateau Monteh-lay-nuh, just north of Calistoga, made by the winemaker Mike Gur-gitch. The best red was the 1973 Cabernet Sauvignon from Stag's Leap Wine Cellars, on the Silverado Trail. Time magazine published the news, and the event became known as the Judgment of Paris, after the Greek myth. A bottle of the Monteh-lay-nuh is now in the Smithsonian, and the story became a 2008 film, Bottle Shock. Chateau Monteh-lay-nuh itself has a fun history. It was founded in 1882 by Alfred Tubbs, who'd made a fortune in rope during the Gold Rush. In 1958 it was bought by a Chinese engineer and his wife, who dug a lake and planted a Chinese garden. And a footnote that's still being argued about: statisticians have re-crunched the numbers ever since. A 2026 analysis by a Master of Wine found arithmetic errors in published totals suggesting the white wine result was actually a tie with a French Meursault, and that by some counting methods Château Haut-Brion was the judges' most consistently preferred red. But history remembers the headline, and Napa's reputation was made.

Driving through these hills, you'll see blackened trunks and new houses where old ones stood. This is the story of the fires. On the night of Sunday the 8th of October 2017, hot, dry Diablo winds were gusting up to seventy miles an hour across Northern California. Over a dozen wildfires broke out that night. One started at 9:43 p.m. near Tubbs Lane, in the rural north of Calistoga. Pushed by north-easterly winds, the front of the Tubbs Fire moved more than twelve miles in its first three hours, through the Mark West Springs area and into the city of Santa Rosa. It destroyed more than 5,600 structures, half of them homes in Santa Rosa, about five percent of the city's housing. At the time it was the most destructive wildfire in California history. Across the region, that month's fires killed 44 people. Cal Fire later concluded that the Tubbs Fire was caused by a private electrical system next to a home, not by the utility. Even so, Pacific Gas and Electric, facing liabilities from other fires, folded the victims' claims into a 13.5-billion-dollar bankruptcy settlement. And here's a haunting detail: the Tubbs Fire followed exactly the same path as the Hanly Fire of 1964. Then came 2020. In August, a freak lightning storm sparked hundreds of fires, and the LNU Lightning Complex burned over 360,000 acres around Napa, Vacka-vill and Fairfield. In September, the Glass Fire started near Deer Park above Saint Huh-lee-nuh and burned over 67,000 acres, destroying 1,555 structures, including wineries, the three-Michelin-star Restaurant at Meadowood, and the historic White Sulphur Springs resort. Calistoga was evacuated for the second time in three years. About sixty percent of the Napa Valley has burned since 2017. The aftermath is still unfolding, and it's about money. From around 2020, seven of California's twelve largest home insurers stopped renewing policies in high-risk areas, saying they weren't allowed to raise rates enough to cover the risk. Homeowners flooded into the state's insurer of last resort, the FAIR Plan, from 124,000 properties in 2019 to 663,000 by March 2026. The state has responded by letting insurers price in future fire risk. So when you see a new house on a burned hillside here, there's a good chance someone fought hard to insure it.

If you can see the big mountain to the north of Calistoga, that's Mount Saint Huh-lee-nuh, the peak that closes off the head of the Napa Valley. It has five summits arranged in a rough letter M. The highest is in Sonoma County, and the next is the high point of Napa County. The Napa River starts on its slopes, and it's one of the few mountains in the Bay Area that gets snow in winter. The Wah-po called it Kanamota, Human Mountain. Spanish colonists called it Mount My-uh-kah-muss. The name it has now comes from an unexpected direction: Russia. In 1841, a Russian survey party from Fort Ross, on the Sonoma coast, climbed the peak and left a copper plate on the summit, inscribed with the date and the name of Princess Huh-lee-nuh de Gagarin, wife of the fort's commanding officer. So the mountain, and very likely the town of Saint Huh-lee-nuh, are named after a Russian aristocrat. Geologically it's made of uplifted volcanic rock, and it has an explosive past. Its eruptions sent pyroclastic flows across this landscape, and one of them, as you're about to hear, turned a forest to stone.

Coming up on Petrified Forest Road is, appropriately, the Petrified Forest. About 3.4 million years ago, a volcanic eruption from the direction of Mount Saint Huh-lee-nuh buried a forest of giant redwoods in volcanic ash. Over thousands of years, the trees turned to stone. It's the only petrified forest in California from the Pliocene, and it claims the largest petrified trees in the world. The biggest, nicknamed The Queen, is eight feet wide and 65 feet long, and was around 2,000 years old when the volcano killed it. The trees are an extinct species of Sequoia, the redwood genus, and they tell us something surprising: redwoods once grew much further inland than they do today. A Berkeley researcher has been studying fossil pollen from the site since 2012. As far as science is concerned, the forest was discovered in 1870 by the palaeontologist Othniel Charles Marsh. Robert Louis Stevenson visited during his 1880 honeymoon and wrote about it in The Silverado Squatters, describing it as owned by an old Swedish ex-sailor who'd stumbled on it while clearing land, and there's a petrified tree named after Stevenson. A woman called Ollie Orre Bockee bought it around 1912 for 14,000 dollars, opened it to tourists two years later at fifty cents a head, and her family has run it ever since. It was damaged in the 2017 fires and has since reopened, and in 2023 it was put up for sale for twelve million dollars.

You're crossing the My-uh-kah-muss Mountains, and almost everything around you was once molten. The rock is called the Sonoma Volcanics: obsidian, pumice, tuff, rhyolite, andesite breccia and basalt lava, several thousand feet thick. It forms most of the mountains around the Napa and Sonoma valleys, and it probably once formed a continuous mass from San Pablo Bay north into Lake County, and from Solano County west to the Santa Rosa plain. Geologists think it erupted from several vents, on and off, over perhaps more than a million years, mostly in the Pliocene, three to five million years ago. It's also the parent material of many of the soils in the Napa and Sonoma wine regions. The volcanic story isn't over. To the north, around Clear Lake, is the Clear Lake Volcanic Field, with lava domes, cinder cones and explosion craters. Its last eruption was only about 11,000 years ago, and the U.S. Geological Survey ranks its threat as high. Its volcanic heat is thought to have driven the hot springs that formed mercury and gold ores around Clear Lake. That heat also powers The Geysers, up in the My-uh-kah-muss north-west of here: the largest geothermal field in the world, with eighteen power plants drawing steam from more than 350 wells. In 2019 it produced around a fifth of California's renewable energy. For something like 12,000 years, Native people built steam baths and thermal pools there for healing and ceremony. In the 1850s it became a resort that drew Ulysses Grant, Theodore Roosevelt and Mark Twain. And despite the name, the steam vents aren't true geysers at all; they're fumaroles. The surveyor who named the place in 1847 got it wrong, and nobody's bothered to change it.

You're coming down through the Mark West Springs area, named after a Scottish-American pioneer, William Marcus West. The springs here were a resort from 1880, perhaps earlier, and Mark West Creek, which you're following, runs nearly thirty miles from the My-uh-kah-muss to the Russian River. On the night of the 8th of October 2017, this valley was directly in the path of the Tubbs Fire, racing west from Calistoga on fierce winds toward Santa Rosa. One story from that night stands out. At Safari West, a 400-acre wildlife preserve nearby, home to giraffes, rhinos, cheetahs and around 800 animals, the 76-year-old owner, Peter Lang, stayed behind and fought the flames by himself for more than ten hours, using only garden hoses. Not a single animal died. Down the hill, the community of Larkfield-Wicky-up lost about 500 homes. Two years later, in 2019, the Kincade Fire started in The Geysers to the north and was pushed by extreme winds right to the edge of the same community, into the Tubbs burn scar. Much of what you see here has been rebuilt since.

The hills north of Santa Rosa have attracted dreamers. In 1875, a religious leader called Thomas Lake Harris brought his followers, the Brotherhood of the New Life, from New York to found a colony called Fountain Grove. His mansion was called Aestivossa, which he said meant high country of divine joy in a language only he understood, and he insisted his real palace was in interspace. The practical side was run by his California lieutenant, Nagasawa Kanaye, who managed 2,000 acres of vineyards and succeeded Harris as leader until 1934. Fountaingrove is now a wealthy neighbourhood; its round barn, a local landmark, burned in the Tubbs Fire. Then in October 1894, about thirty Christian socialists led by a Berkeley Unitarian minister, Edward Payne, founded Al-true-ree-uh, a commune in these hills inspired by a utopian novel, A Traveller from Al-true-ree-uh. They grew orchards, sold produce in San Francisco and built a hotel. The hotel sank them. Within a year they needed a bankruptcy plan, and by 1896 every Altrurian settlement was abandoned.

West of the freeway, River Road passes the little community of Fulton, founded by the brothers Thomas and James Fulton, with a post office since 1871. The commuter trains of the SMART line run through it today. Ahead, the land flattens into the floodplain of the Laguna de Santa Rosa, a 22-mile-long wetland that drains most of the Santa Rosa plain. In heavy winter rain it spreads out into a shallow lake that can hold over 80,000 acre-feet of stormwater, an enormous natural sponge. It's the most biologically diverse place in Sonoma County, with over 200 species of birds, bald and golden eagles, otters, mink and bobcats, and three endangered plants found nowhere else. It's also, sadly, listed as the most impaired water body on California's North Coast, after more than a century of farming and building on its floodplain, though restoration began in the 1990s. There's a hydrological oddity here too. Mark West Creek, which we followed down from the hills, has been diverted in three places near its meeting with the Laguna, so that it looks as if the creek feeds the Laguna, when naturally it's the other way round.

Welcome to the Russian River, the last leg of the journey. It's the second-largest river in the Bay Area after the Sacramento, with a main stem 115 miles long, flowing south from Mendocino County and then west to the Pacific. It has had a lot of names. The Southern Poe-moe called it Ashokawna, east water place, and also Bidapte, big river. A Spanish land grant of 1843 called it the Rio Grande. Its current name comes from the Russian-American Company, which ran the fur-trading colony at Fort Ross on the coast in the early 1800s. A Russian explorer, Ivan Kuskov, travelled up the river, and an 1817 Russian chart calls it the Slavyanka. This is also the Russian River Valley wine appellation, created in 1983: cool, foggy country, because of the valley's closeness to the Pacific. That suits Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, the grapes it's famous for. Vines came here with Mediterranean immigrants in the late 1800s, and by 1900 there were nearly 200 wineries in the region. Before the vines, the river's banks were lined with redwoods, which drew loggers in the late nineteenth century. You'll see the second-growth forest close in as we head downstream.

The land around Forestville and Meer-uh-bell was once Rancho El Molino, the Ranch of the Mill. It was granted in 1833 to John Bautista Rogers Cooper, a sea captain who'd married General Vuh-lay-oh's sister. The grant had a strategic purpose: the Mexican authorities wanted settlers pushing west toward the coast to counter the Russian presence at Fort Ross. In 1834 Cooper built a water-powered sawmill here, driven by Mark West Creek and cutting redwood. It's recognised as the first water-powered commercial sawmill in California. The river had the last word, though: floods destroyed it in the winter of 1840 to 41. Forestville itself was settled in the late 1860s, originally spelled with two r's, after one of its founders. By 1900 it had a bohemian reputation as a gathering place for writers and artists.

This lovely, lazy river has a violent side. Flood stage at Gurn-vill is 32 feet, and in the second half of the twentieth century the river topped it about five times a decade. The record is 49.5 feet, in February 1986. January 1995 hit 48 feet. Two big dams upstream, Coyote Valley Dam, built in 1959, forming Lake Mendocino, and Warm Springs Dam, finished in 1982, forming Lake Sonoma, now hold back some of the flood water, and flooding is less frequent. But in February 2019 the river rose to levels comparable to 1986. And here's a water fight in the making. Part of the Russian River's summer flow doesn't belong to this river at all. Since 1908, a tunnel in the mountains of Mendocino County, the Potter Valley Project, has diverted water from the Eel River into the headwaters of the Russian. A dam built on the Eel in 1922 lets it keep flowing in summer. That borrowed water helps supply Sonoma Water, which provides Russian River water to more than 600,000 people in Sonoma and Marin counties. But in 2019 the owner, Pacific Gas and Electric, decided the old hydro plant wasn't worth relicensing. The Eel River dams are to be removed, and the Russian River communities are working out how to keep some of that water coming.

On the riverbank near Ree-oh Nee-doh is Kor-bell, which has made sparkling wine here since 1882. It was founded by Francis Kor-bell and his brothers, emigrants from Bohemia, who'd also founded a satirical San Francisco magazine called The Wasp. They used the traditional Champagne method, where the wine is fermented a second time in the very bottle you buy. Kor-bell still prints the word champagne on its labels, which might make a Frenchman wince. It's legal because of U.S. rules from the 1930s that treat certain place names as semi-generic, as long as the label also says where the grapes really grew, and a 2006 trade agreement with the European Union protected older American brands that already used it. The Heck family bought the company in 1954 and grew it into one of the biggest wine producers in the country, at 1.6 million cases a year.

Ree-oh Nee-doh, the river nest, is a little resort village tucked into a redwood canyon. In 1908 a San Francisco fraternal lodge, the Eagles, bought the land and divided it among members, and the place was first called Eaglenest. During the Second World War its dance hall heaved with sailors on liberty and troops heading for the Pacific, and big bands played there. A small excursion boat once ran down the river to Gurn-vill's beach. Two local oddities. The town's unofficial slogan is The Moon Is Always Out In Ree-oh Nee-doh. And its roads are named Canyon One, Two, Three, Four, Six and Seven. There is no Canyon Five, the story goes, because of an accident on the road that became Canyon Six.

Welcome to Gurn-vill, and congratulations, you've made it. First, the name: it's said Gurn-vill, and locals sell T-shirts reading Don't call it Guerneyville, although people have been saying it that way since the 1800s. The local Poe-moe used this spot as a summer camp and called it Ceola, the shady place. The redwoods here grew so thickly that local lore says the valley once had the greatest density of living matter on the planet. Then came the loggers. So many trees were cut in the late 1800s that the town's first English name was Stumptown, and the demand for lumber to rebuild San Francisco after the 1906 earthquake made the logging boom. The present name honours George Guerne, a Swiss immigrant who owned the sawmill. The annual parade is still called Stumptown Days. And the forests you see on the hills are mostly less than 200 years old, regrowth after the logging. In 1877 the railroad connected the town to the San Francisco ferries, and Gurn-vill became a summer playground for the city. Jet travel in the 1960s and the 1964 floods hit the old resorts hard. Then in the late 1970s, gay entrepreneurs from San Francisco discovered the area, and their weekends revived the town. It's been known for its liberal, welcoming atmosphere ever since. In summer, fog rolls up the river from the Pacific, and the drip from the fog keeps the redwoods and ferns lush.

Just north of town is Armstrong Redwoods State Natural Reserve, 805 acres of coast redwoods, including old-growth forest. In the 1870s, Colonel James Armstrong set the grove aside as a natural park. After his death his daughter and another local family campaigned with meetings, rallies and car caravans to save this last remnant of the old forest, and in 1917 Sonoma County bought it for 80,000 dollars. The tallest tree, the Parson Jones Tree, is more than 310 feet high and about a hundred yards from the entrance. The oldest, the Colonel Armstrong Tree, is estimated at over 1,400 years old. The reserve gets about 55 inches of rain a year, almost all between September and June, and in summer the fog keeps it damp. If you have an hour to spare after the drive, there's an easy, wheelchair-accessible trail through the grove.

Just downstream at Mon-tee Ree-oh, hidden in the redwoods, is the Bo-hee-mee-un Grove: a 2,700-acre private campground owned by San Francisco's Bo-hee-mee-un Club. Every July it hosts an encampment of more than two weeks for invited members and guests from politics, business and the arts. It started innocently. The club was founded in 1872 by newspaper journalists, and in 1878 fewer than a hundred members held an overnight send-off in the Marin redwoods for an actor who was moving to New York. They enjoyed it so much they did it again the next year without him, and it became tradition. From 1893 they camped here, and in 1899 they bought the grove from a logging company that had preserved a stand of old-growth redwoods. Soon wealthy San Francisco businessmen joined, and the money and power followed. Its most famous moment: in September 1942, the grove hosted a meeting on the early planning of the Manhattan Project, with Ernest Lawrence and J. Robert Oppenheimer, which fed into the development of the atomic bomb. In July 1950, Dwight Eisenhower and Richard Nixon first met there, at a lunch hosted by Herbert Hoover. No woman has ever been granted full membership. And the secrecy breeds legends: in 2000 the broadcaster Alex Jones sneaked in and filmed the annual Cremation of Care ceremony and called it a ritual sacrifice, a claim other reporting doesn't support; the documentary-maker Jon Ronson, using the same footage, compared it to an overgrown frat party. One of the grove's camps, by the way, is named Silverado Squatters, after Stevenson's book. Mon-tee Ree-oh itself began as a railroad stop shipping redwood lumber to build San Francisco, then reinvented itself as a vacation wonderland, with a seven-storey hotel. Parts of the 1942 film Holiday Inn were shot here.

The Russian River is Poe-moe country. The Poe-moe lands once stretched from the Pacific coast inland to Clear Lake, but the Poe-moe were never one nation. They lived in small, independent bands, linked by family and marriage, and spoke seven related languages so different that speakers of one couldn't understand another. Linguists think their ancestors may have reached the Clear Lake uplands thousands of years ago, and later spread into the Russian River valley. The name itself is a happy accident of history. In one Poe-moe language, it meant something like those who live at red earth hole, the name of a single village in Potter Valley, perhaps after the red magnesite mined there for beads, or the reddish, iron-rich soil. By 1877 English speakers were using it for the whole people. Along the lower Russian River lived speakers of Southern Poe-moe. As the southernmost Poe-moe, they were the first to suffer from Spanish colonisation, and Southern Poe-moe people were used as labour to build the last of the California missions, at Sonoma. The American period that followed made things worse. By the time linguists came to record the language, only the northern groups survived, and in 2012 there was just one fluent speaker left. Since 2011 the Dry Creek Rancheria has run a revitalisation programme, with classes, a mobile app and signs on ancestral land. Today, several rancherias, small reservations, carry on: Dry Creek, Cloverdale, Lytton and Grayton among them. And the language lives in the landscape. The Southern Poe-moe name for this river is Ashokawna, east water place, and their old Coyote stories mention the beavers that once dammed it.

You've turned north onto Interstate 505, a quiet four-lane spur that runs about thirty miles up the western edge of the Sacramento Valley to Interstate 5. It exists so that traffic between the Bay Area and the far north of California can bypass Sacramento entirely. It has an odd backstory. It was originally planned as part of a looping interstate called I-5W, with a W for west. The federal highway authorities later scrapped almost all of those lettered interstates, so I-5W was chopped up and renumbered: part of it became I-580, part became the stretch of I-80 you just drove, and this part became 505. The northernmost section only opened in 1977. Out of the window, you're on the flat alluvial fans at the foot of the Vacka Mountains, the ridge to your left. Geologists' maps show patches of the Tuh-hay-muh Formation here, river sediments and volcanic ash a few million years old, the last layers laid down before these hills rose.

Winters, coming up, sits on Pew-tah Creek where it leaves the hills, and it's one of the places where farming in the Sacramento Valley began. In 1842, William Wolfskill, a Kentuckian who'd settled in Mexican California, was granted Rancho Rio de los Poo-toss along the creek. His brother John started planting orchards and vineyards on the land, and is credited with beginning the agricultural development of the whole Sacramento Valley. The town came later: its post office opened in 1875, and it's named after Theodore Winters, whose ranch provided half of the town's land. The Wolfskill connection lasts to this day. In 1935, the family's heirs gave a hundred acres of the old ranch to the University of California at Davis for an experimental orchard. Here we leave the interstate and follow Highway 128 west, up Pew-tah Creek into the hills.

The creek beside the road is Pew-tah Creek, eighty-five miles long, from the My-uh-kah-muss Mountains to the Yo-lo Bypass. Its name has been argued over for a century and a half. Spanish-era records called it the Arroyo de los Poo-toss, and for a while it was mapped as Puta Creek, until the federal naming board rejected that spelling, probably because of its resemblance to a rude Spanish word. The place-name scholar Erwin Gudde concluded the resemblance is purely accidental, and that the name comes from the Lake Mee-wok words for grassy creek. The Pat-win name for it is Liwaito. The creek has also been the scene of one of California's quieter environmental victories. It's dammed twice: at Monti-sello Dam up ahead, and at the little Pew-tah Diversion Dam, which forms Lake Solano and sends water down a 33-mile canal to farms and to the cities of Vuh-lay-oh and Benicia. After the drought years of the late 1980s, most of Pew-tah Creek below the dams went dry. That prompted a landmark lawsuit, and in 2000 the parties signed the Pew-tah Creek Accord, guaranteeing water releases that mimic natural flows, higher in winter and spring, lower in summer. The results have been striking: riparian bird species have doubled, and native steelhead trout and Chinook salmon have returned to spawn, while the farmers downstream keep their water.

These dry, grassy canyons burn often, and Highway 128 has been closed by fire again and again. In July 2015, the Wragg Fire started right beside the highway near Lake Berry-essa, and the cause was mundane: the hot exhaust of an idling vehicle touching dry grass. It forced the evacuation of 136 homes and closed both this road and Interstate 505. In July 2017, the Winters Fire broke out a few miles south-west of Winters. In June 2020, the Quail Fire burned nearly 2,000 acres in Quail Canyon, between Winters and Vacka-vill. Then, in August 2020, came the big one. A highly unusual series of thunderstorms, fed by moisture from a dying tropical storm, sparked fires all over Northern California. Around here alone there was the Markley Fire near Monti-sello Dam, another near the Pew-tah Creek bridge, the Spanish Fire at Spanish Flat and the Gamble Fire north of the lake. With firefighters stretched across the state, they grew unchecked and merged with the Hennessy Fire into the LNU Lightning Complex, which burned over 363,000 acres across five counties.

Look up the canyon for Monti-sello Dam, a 304-foot concrete arch wedged into a narrow gorge known as Devil's Gate. It's a hundred feet thick at the base and just twelve at the top, and it was built between 1953 and 1957. When the last bucket of concrete was poured, on the 26th of February 1957, the crew followed tradition and tossed in a few coins. The dam's claim to fame is its spillway, known as the Glory Hole. Instead of a channel over the side, there's a giant concrete funnel in the lake, 72 feet across at the lip, that drops 200 feet straight down through the hillside. When the lake is full, water pours into it like an enormous bathtub drain. It doesn't happen often: it overflowed in 2017 for the first time since 2006, and again in 2019. It is genuinely dangerous; in 1997 a woman was pulled in and killed. Behind the dam lies Lake Berry-essa, the largest lake in Napa County, about sixteen miles long with 165 miles of shoreline. It was built to irrigate the farms of Solano and Yo-lo counties, and it supplies water and a little hydroelectric power to the North Bay. A curiosity: the dam and lake are entirely in Napa County, but the dam is less than 500 feet from the Yo-lo and Solano county lines.

Under Lake Berry-essa lies a whole town. The valley was once Rancho Las Putas, granted in 1843 to two members of the Berry-essa family, a prominent Californio family, which is where the lake gets its name. They lost much of it fast: by 1853 they were selling land to pay gambling debts, and when they couldn't pay a 1,645-dollar debt in cash, a creditor got the county to auction 26,000 acres. He bought it for 2,000 dollars and sold it for 100,000. In 1866 developers laid out a town called Monti-sello. Farmers poured in, growing wheat and barley on what was considered some of the finest soil in the country. It had hotels, blacksmiths, a general store, and a stagecoach stop for the quicksilver miners from Knoxville to the north. In 1896 a three-arched stone bridge was built over Pew-tah Creek, at 298 feet the largest stone bridge west of the Rockies. People had talked about damming the valley since 1906, and in 1947 Solano County and the federal Bureau of Reclamation launched the Solano Project. Monti-sello's residents protested, but Governor Earl Warren backed the dam, and the town was doomed. The photographers Dorothea Lange and Pirkle Jones documented its death for Life magazine, though Life never ran the story. Buildings were razed to their foundations, orchards cut down, and the cemetery moved to a bluff called Spanish Flat. The post office closed in 1956. But the old stone bridge was too well built to demolish easily, so they left it. It's still down there, under the water.

Now for some roadside geology, because the cuts along Highway 128 here are a slice through time. The layered sandstones and shales you've been passing are the Great Valley Sequence, the same ancient sea-floor deposits that lie miles beneath the flat valley behind you. Here, on the valley's western margin, they come to the surface. On the Macrostrat geological maps, this canyon shows a run of named formations from the Late Cretaceous, the last age of the dinosaurs: the Sites, Venado and Yo-lo formations. The Venado is a massive greenish-grey sandstone, and near Monti-sello Dam its base includes a layer of megabreccia, a jumble of angular blocks. The Yo-lo Formation's mudstones contain microscopic fossils, radiolarians and foraminifera, that date it to the Coniacian stage of the Late Cretaceous, roughly 88 million years ago. These were deep-sea fans: sand and mud that poured down underwater canyons off the ancient Sierra and settled on the ocean floor. So each time the road cuts through one of these beds, you're looking at the bottom of a Cretaceous sea.

Watch the roadcuts and hillsides for a change in colour: greenish, shiny, slippery-looking rock and thin, scrubby vegetation. According to the Macrostrat maps, this stretch of Highway 128 crosses the Coast Range Ophiolite, and the rock here is serpentinised peridotite. That's a remarkable thing to drive past. Peridotite is a dense rock derived from the Earth's mantle, rich in the green mineral olivine. An off-ee-oh-lite is a section of ocean crust and the upper mantle beneath it that has been uplifted and pushed onto continental rocks. When sea water is forced deep into rock like this, it turns it into serpentinite. The Coast Range Ophiolite is Middle to Late Jurassic in age, older than the sea-floor sandstones you've just passed, and it's described as arguably the most extensive off-ee-oh-lite in the United States. Next, the road crosses into the Franciscan rocks to the west. Serpentine soils are low in calcium relative to magnesium, poor in nutrients and high in heavy metals like chromium and nickel, which makes life very hard for plants. That's why the slopes look sparse, and why this region is home to rare plants found nowhere else. The Berry-essa Snow Mountain National Monument, which surrounds this lake country, describes them as delicate serpentine plants clinging to otherwise barren mountainsides.

The wild hills around Lake Berry-essa are part of the Berry-essa Snow Mountain National Monument, proclaimed by President Obama in July 2015 under the Antiquities Act. It stretches about a hundred miles north from here into Mendocino County, over 340,000 acres of the inner Coast Ranges, with bald and golden eagles, black bears, mountain lions and tule elk. These hills have been home to many Native peoples for around 11,000 years: Pat-win, Poe-moe, Wah-po, Lake Mee-wok, Yuki and others. The politics are interesting. A broad coalition of counties, cities, the state legislature, a Poe-moe tribe and conservation groups campaigned for it. But the lake itself was deliberately left out, because boaters worried that a monument might one day restrict their motorboats and jet skis. In May 2024, President Biden expanded the monument by nearly 14,000 acres to include an eleven-mile ridge called Molok Luyuk.

Much of the Coast Ranges, from here west to the ocean, is built of one of the strangest rock assemblages on Earth: the Franciscan Complex. For tens of millions of years, from the Jurassic onward, an ocean plate dived beneath the edge of North America. As it went down, it scraped off a chaotic mixture of material: deep-sea sandstone called gray-wacky, chert containing the fossils of tiny radiolaria, basalt from the ocean floor, and slices of rock that had been dragged deep down and squeezed under enormous pressure before popping back up.
