Geologists call the mashed-up result an accretionary wedge, and the Franciscan is the classic example. It's the ridge that acted as a dam on the west side of the ancient Great Valley sea. The Macrostrat maps of the roads you'll drive today show all its flavours. Graywacke sandstone and shale in the hills of Sage Canyon. Mélange, a rock that looks like a fruitcake, with blocks of chert, greenstone, serpentinite and blueschist floating in a sheared, muddy matrix. And blueschist itself, a rare blue rock with the mineral glaucophane, that only forms at high pressure but low temperature, exactly the conditions deep in a subduction zone. Along the Russian River, the maps show blueschist-facies metabasalt and metagraywacke. If you see a blue-grey, shiny rock in a road cut over there, you may be looking at old ocean floor that went down into a subduction zone and somehow came back. And look closely at the geological maps of these hills and you'll see them dotted with mapped landslides.

The lake beside you now is Lake Hennessy, the City of Napa's main water supply. Congress authorised a dam here in 1944 to protect Napa from floods, but never paid for it, so in 1946 the city built Conn Creek Dam itself, for 550,000 dollars, plus thirty miles of pipe made by the Basalt Rock Company south of Napa. It's named after Edwin Hennessy, a local civic leader who helped develop it. The name has a second meaning now. Early on the morning of the 17th of August 2020, a lightning-sparked spot fire was reported on Hennessy Ridge Road near this lake. The Hennessy Fire grew to 192,000 acres on its own, the heart of the LNU Lightning Complex. Hidden in the hills to the north are two little-visited valleys. Chill-eez Valley, named after Joseph Chill-eez, who got a Mexican land grant in 1843 and planted vines there in 1850, is now its own small wine appellation, cooler than the main valley. And Pope Valley, beyond it, has a surprising film credit: in the summer of 1978, the opening skydiving sequence of the James Bond film Moonraker was shot in the skies above it.

California's history is in large part a history of moving water, and Lake Berry-essa is a textbook case. The farms of Solano and Yo-lo counties had been worked since the 1840s, but summer brought no reliable rain. As early as 1907, Bay Area cities hired three engineers, including George Washington Goethals and Arthur Powell Davis, to study damming Pew-tah Creek; the result was known as the Mulholland-Goethals-Davis plan. The cities' interest moved on to bigger schemes. In the 1940s, Solano County's water council chose the Devil's Gate site, and in 1947 the county and the U.S. Bureau of Reclamation launched the Solano Project, with Governor Earl Warren pushing it as essential for growth. It was designed to give a full irrigation supply to 96,000 acres of prime farmland. The lake behind Monti-sello Dam can hold 1.6 million acre-feet, and about 375,000 acre-feet of runoff flow in each year. Downstream, the Pew-tah Diversion Dam sends water south in the Pew-tah South Canal to farms and to the taps of Vuh-lay-oh and Benicia. By one estimate the dam prevented about five million dollars of flood damage between 1957 and 1995. The costs fell on the valley's residents, who lost their town, and on the creek itself, which ran dry below the dams in the drought of the late 1980s, until a lawsuit and the Pew-tah Creek Accord of 2000 guaranteed it water of its own. It's a small-scale version of the bargain behind every big California water project: cities and farms gain, someone's valley is flooded, and the fish wait for the lawyers.

You're crossing Los Car-nair-ohss, the low, rolling hills between the Napa and Sonoma valleys, along the top of San Pablo Bay. Car-nair-ohss is Spanish for rams, after the sheep that once grazed these hills, and the name goes back to a Mexican land grant of 1836, Rancho Rincón de los Car-nair-ohss. This is a wine region with an unusual distinction: it was the first in California to be defined by its climate rather than by political boundaries. Being so close to the bay, it gets fog and cool breezes, so it's cooler and more moderate than the valleys to the north. That suits Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, and a lot of the grapes here go into sparkling wine. Which explains the French château you may see on a hilltop: Domaine Car-nair-ohss, founded in 1987 by the Champagne house Taittinger, and modelled on Taittinger's own Château de la Marquetterie in Champagne. The road you're on, today's Highways 12 and 121, was the old Sonoma Highway that linked the two valleys, travelled by settlers in search of farmland and by miners in the Gold Rush.

Hidden off this road is the di Rosa Center for Contemporary Art, and the land has had quite a life. In 1855 it was planted with grapes and olives. In 1886 two Frenchmen built a stone winery. Then phylloxera killed the vines, and the old winery was used for growing mushrooms, making moonshine, storing grain and finally as a hay barn. In 1960 Rene di Rosa bought it, replanted vines, and dammed an old irrigation pond, dug by Depression-era WPA workers, into a 35-acre lake. His Winery Lake vineyards eventually covered some 250 acres, and when he sold them to Seagram in 1986, he used the money to turn the property into an art park. Today it holds about 1,600 works by Northern California artists, scattered through galleries and a sculpture meadow, and the land is protected forever by the county land trust.

Here's a fun one. Somewhere around here, near the Napa and Sonoma county line on this very highway, is the hill in what may be the most viewed photograph in history: Bliss, the default wallpaper of Windows XP. That bright green hill under a blue sky with wispy clouds. In January 1996, Charles O'Rear, a former National Geographic photographer who lived in Saint Huh-lee-nuh, was driving along the Sonoma Highway to visit his girlfriend. A storm had just passed, the winter rains had turned the grass a vivid green, and he noticed a hill that had been cleared of its vines after a phylloxera infestation. He pulled over, set up a medium-format camera on a tripod with saturated Fuji Velvia film, and took four shots. He says he didn't manipulate it at all. It started life as a stock photo called Bucolic Green Hills. Bill Gates's photo agency Corbis acquired it, and Microsoft bought the full rights in 2000. Photographers have tried to recreate the shot ever since, but they can't, because the hill has gone back to being a vineyard. So look out for green hills with vines on them: one of them might be the most famous hill in the world, wearing a disguise.

This crossroads is Schellville, named after Theodore Schell, who ranched nearby. It's been an important railway junction since 1888, and a two-mile-long railyard sits just south of the old depot, which is now the freight office for the SMART line. Being low beside Sonoma Creek, it floods every five to ten years in a wet winter. In March 2023, after months of rain, the waterlogged ground gave way and a train carrying corn seed derailed here, toppling four cars. Nobody was hurt. On the way into Sonoma there's another kind of railroad: Sonoma TrainTown, a quarter-scale railway on fifteen-inch track. Stanley Frank of Oakland started building it in 1958, making everything himself, from the houses and landscaping to the steam locomotives. It opened in 1968 and the family still runs it: a twenty-minute ride past waterfalls and tiny detailed houses, over a trestle and through tunnels, on four miles of track.

Welcome to Sonoma, where modern California arguably began. When the Spanish arrived, this was near the meeting point of several Native peoples: the Coast Mee-wok, the Southern Poe-moe to the north-west, the Wah-po to the north-east, and the Pat-win to the east. In 1823, a Franciscan priest, José Altimira, founded Mission San Francisco Solano here. It was the twenty-first, last and northernmost of the California missions, and the only one built after Mexico won independence from Spain. Part of the point was political: the governor wanted a presence north of the bay to block the Russians, who had a colony at Fort Ross on the coast. When Mexico secularised the missions in the 1830s, a young officer called Mariano Guadalupe Vuh-lay-oh was sent to close this one and turn it into a town. In 1835 he laid out the plaza you'll see in the centre, the largest town plaza in California, with soldiers' barracks on one side. The City Hall in the middle, dedicated in 1908, was built with four identical faces so that none of the merchants around the square would feel snubbed. The mission, the barracks and Vuh-lay-oh's later home are now part of Sonoma State Historic Park.

Across from the mission is the Blue Wing Inn, one of the first hotels north of San Francisco. It started with the very first property deal in the new town: Vuh-lay-oh gave the lot to his majordomo, Antonio Ortega, who managed the closing of the mission. The parish priest soon complained about Ortega's treatment of the Native people, and in 1837, after more scandals and doubtful accounts, Vuh-lay-oh removed him. Ortega stayed on and ran a tavern there until 1848. In 1849, at the height of the Gold Rush, two men bought it and turned it into a hotel with a gambling hall and a saloon, serving miners heading to and from the gold fields and the American soldiers stationed in Sonoma. The State of California bought it in 1968.

Sonoma's plaza is where California's strangest little rebellion happened. By 1846, Mexico had largely neglected its distant province of Alta California, and Mexican officials were nervous about the growing number of Americans arriving without permission. Those immigrants, in turn, complained they weren't allowed to buy land and had been threatened with expulsion. Meanwhile, a U.S. Army explorer, Captain John C. Frémont, was camped in the Sacramento Valley, quietly encouraging trouble. At dawn on the 14th of June 1846, a band of about thirty-three American settlers rode into Sonoma and took General Vuh-lay-oh prisoner. Vuh-lay-oh, who was actually sympathetic to the idea of American rule, negotiated the terms of his surrender with them, while, according to accounts, the rebels proceeded to get drunk. They raised a homemade flag with a grizzly bear and the words California Republic, and declared independence. The republic lasted about three and a half weeks. Meanwhile, the Mexican-American War had broken out. On the 9th of July, a U.S. Navy lieutenant, Joseph Revere, raised the American flag in front of the Sonoma barracks, and the Bear Flag Republic was over. Vuh-lay-oh later wrote, in effect, that if the rebels had simply raised the Stars and Stripes, there would have been no war on the Sonoma frontier, because the Californios had been ready to welcome the Americans. The bear flag, though, survived. It became the basis of California's state flag, and a monument on the plaza marks the spot where it was first raised. The boulder it stands on was hauled in from a mile away.

One man appears in almost every story on this side of the hills: Mariano Guadalupe Vuh-lay-oh. Let's meet him properly. He was born in Monterey in 1807, the eighth of thirteen children of a Spanish soldier. As a boy he and two other promising youngsters were given private lessons by the governor, with access to his library and newspapers from Mexico City, and an English merchant taught him English, French and Latin. He joined the presidio company as a cadet, and in his twenties was sent north to close the Sonoma mission and command the northern frontier, keeping the Native peoples and the Russians in check. He became enormously powerful and rich. His influence helped others win land grants, including the American settler George Yount in the Napa Valley. He was granted Rancho Petaluma, 44,000 acres. The mission lands were supposed to go partly to the Native people who'd worked them, and at first he did give some to them, but later he took it all into his own rancho. He was a man in the middle of two worlds. In 1846 the Bear Flaggers took him prisoner, even though he favoured American annexation. He took part in California's 1849 constitutional convention and served in the first State Senate. The city of Vuh-lay-oh is named after him, and Benicia after his wife, Francisca Benicia Carrillo. In the 1850s he built a home just outside Sonoma, a prefabricated wooden Gothic house shipped round Cape Horn, with bricks inside the walls for insulation. He called it Lachryma Montis, mountain tear, a Latin rendering of the Native name for the spring on the property, which meant crying mountain. He lived at Lachryma Montis from 1852 until his death in 1890, and you can still visit it.

Sonoma Valley calls itself the birthplace of the California wine industry, and there's a case for it. The Franciscan friars planted the valley's first vines at the mission in 1823, and Vuh-lay-oh expanded them. Then came Ah-go-stone Hair-uss-tee, one of the great characters of the West. A Hungarian nobleman, he'd already founded a village in Wisconsin, where German settlers called him Count, and been the first town marshal and county sheriff of San Diego. In 1857, just east of Sonoma, he founded Buena Vista, one of California's first successful commercial wineries. He's often called the father of California wine, and he introduced more than 300 varieties of European grapes. His finances were less impressive than his vision: San Francisco bankers had to take over, and he was forced out in 1866. Buena Vista's original hand-dug caves are still there. Next door, a Bavarian, Jacob Gundlach, planted a vineyard called Rhinefarm in 1858. Gundlach Bundschu is now the oldest winery in California continuously owned by the same family, run by the sixth generation. The 1906 earthquake destroyed its San Francisco cellars and a million gallons of wine. And one more Sonoma first, which may have saved the whole industry: when phylloxera began ravaging California's vineyards in the late 1800s, a Sonoma Valley grower called Julius Dresel pioneered the first commercially successful grafting of European vines onto disease-resistant native American rootstock. That's the technique that rescued California wine.

North of Sonoma, the highway runs through a string of communities known together as the Springs: Boyes Hot Springs, Fetters Hot Springs, Agua Caliente and El Verano. Agua Caliente means hot water. The springs were used and considered sacred by Native people long before the Mexican government granted the land as Rancho Agua Caliente in 1840. In 1895, a Captain Boyes drilled and struck 112-degree water just 70 feet down, and built a resort hotel. It burned in a wildfire in September 1923, along with much of Boyes Springs. Its replacement, a mission-style hotel that opened in 1927, became the Sonoma Mission Inn. During the Second World War the Navy leased it as a rest centre for sailors and Marines back from combat in the Pacific. In March 1943, ninety veterans of Guadalcanal arrived, swapping one of the most brutal battles in American history for soft beds, a golf course, cherry pie and dances.

Off to the west, near the village of Eldridge, are the grounds of the Sonoma Developmental Center, which for over a century was a large state institution for people with developmental disabilities. It opened here in 1891 as the California Home for the Care and Training of Feeble Minded Children, and Jack London, who lived nearby, set a short story there. Its history includes one of the darkest chapters of American public health. California passed a compulsory sterilisation law in 1909, the third state to do so. From 1918, the superintendent here, F. O. Butler, was a firm believer in sterilisation, and personally performed at least a thousand operations. Under him, the institution even admitted people solely to sterilise and release them. It was said to have sterilised more people deemed mental defectives than any other institution in the world. Dangerous medical experiments on residents continued into the 1960s. The centre finally closed at the end of 2018.

Up on the slopes of Sonoma Mountain, above the village of Glen Ellen, is the ranch of the writer Jack London. London's life before Sonoma was the stuff of his books. Born in San Francisco in 1876, he was an oyster pirate in the bay as a teenager, sailed to the Klondike gold rush at 21, and came back a committed socialist. In 1903 he sold The Call of the Wild to a magazine for 750 dollars. In 1905 he bought an abandoned winery here and called it Beauty Ranch. He hoped to become a rancher, and between 1909 and 1911 he bought more land to expand it. Then he began his dream house, Wolf House: 26 rooms, nine fireplaces, built of massive stone to survive earthquakes, with modern marvels like electric light, refrigeration and a built-in vacuum system. He and his wife Charmian poured over 80,000 dollars into it. On the 22nd of August 1913, just before they were due to move in, it burned down. London was devastated and deep in debt, and worked furiously to keep the ranch going. He died there in November 1916, aged forty, of a cause still disputed today. His ashes lie under a rock from the ruins of Wolf House. He named a novel after this place: The Valley of the Moon, a translation of the Native name for the Sonoma Valley. The ranch is now Jack London State Historic Park, and you can walk to the stone shell of Wolf House. Glen Ellen itself was named by an early vineyard owner, Charles Stuart, after his wife Ellen. Hunter S. Thompson lived here for a while too. In October 2017, the Nuns Fire severely damaged the whole village.

A geology note for this stretch, because the Sonoma Valley is lined with volcanic glass. The Macrostrat geological maps show, near Glen Ellen and Kenwood, the Glen Ellen Formation: river gravel, sand and silt made mostly of eroded Sonoma Volcanics, and characterised by pebbles of obsidian, natural volcanic glass. Ash layers in it date to roughly 2.5 to 3.3 million years ago. In the hills, the maps show the Rhyolite of Adobe Canyon, glassy grey-to-white lava with contorted, folded flow bands, dated to about 5.3 million years old. Adobe Canyon Road, near Kenwood, leads up into Sugarloaf Ridge State Park. That obsidian mattered to people. On the north side of the valley, in Trione-Anna-dell State Park, the rocks shaped the whole human history of the place: Native Americans used its obsidian for tools, and in the early 1900s the park's volcanic rock was quarried for cobblestones. Some biologists consider Anna-dell's oak woodland the best undisturbed example of northern oak woodland anywhere. The 2017 Nuns Fire burned its southern part, and the 2020 Glass Fire its northern edge.

Kenwood sits on what was Rancho Los Gee-lee-kose, a Mexican grant of 1837 to a Scottish sea captain, John Wilson, who never lived on it. In 1850 he sold it to another Scot, William Hood, a cabinet-maker who had climbed the mountain above the valley, fallen for the view, and made his fortune building houses in Gold Rush San Francisco to buy it. The peak is now Hood Mountain. When the railroad came in 1887 and 1888, the little town tried on name after name: Rohrerville, after a land company owner, then Los Gee-lee-kose, then South Los Gee-lee-kose. Residents complained Gee-lee-kose was too hard to say, and around 1895 they voted for Kenwood, either because settlers came from Kenwood, Illinois, or because English families knew Kenwood House in London, or perhaps both. A Utah senator, Thomas Kearns, had a ranch here and is said to have entertained President Theodore Roosevelt. Up to the north-east is Sugarloaf Ridge State Park, where the Wah-po lived along Sonoma Creek for some 1,500 years. When the state planned to close it in 2011 to save money, a volunteer group called Team Sugarloaf took it over and reopened it in 2012. It has a volunteer-run observatory, too.

You're in Santa Rosa, the largest city in California's wine country and the county seat of Sonoma County. Before Europeans arrived, the Santa Rosa plain was home to a powerful Poe-moe group called the Bitakomtara, who controlled the area tightly: outsiders needed permission to pass, and faced harsh penalties if they didn't ask. They gathered for ceremonies on Santa Rosa Creek, near today's Spring Lake. Colonisation brought violence, land seizure, enslavement and smallpox, and the population was devastated, though descendants of the survivors still live in the region. The first permanent European home here was built in the 1830s by the family of María López de Carrillo, a widow from San Diego whose daughter had married General Vuh-lay-oh. With his help she was granted Rancho Cabeza de Santa Rosa in 1841, and her adobe stood just east of today's downtown. Before that, Mexican settlers from Sonoma slaughtered cattle where Santa Rosa Creek meets Matanzas Creek, and the name stuck: matanza means slaughter. In the 1850s her son Julio helped lay out the downtown grid around a central square, the pattern the city still follows.

Near downtown Santa Rosa is the house and garden of Luther Burbank, one of the most famous plant breeders who ever lived. He was born in Massachusetts in 1849, the thirteenth of fifteen children. As a young man on a small farm there, he developed a new potato, sold the rights for 150 dollars, and used the money to come to Santa Rosa in 1875. Here, inspired by Charles Darwin's writing on plant and animal breeding, he set up greenhouses and experimental fields and crossed plants on a huge scale. Over 55 years he developed more than 800 strains and varieties: the Shasta daisy, the Santa Rosa plum, the Flaming Gold nectarine, a white blackberry and a spineless cactus for cattle feed. His most consequential creation came almost by accident. A natural variant of his potato, with russet skin, became the Russet Burbank, now the most widely grown potato in the United States and the world's leading potato for food processing. If you've eaten McDonald's fries, there's a good chance you've eaten a Luther Burbank. He lived here for over fifty years, and he's buried in the garden under a cedar of Lebanon.

Santa Rosa was the home of Charles Schulz, creator of Peanuts, Charlie Brown and Snoopy. Schulz grew up in Saint Paul, Minnesota, the son of a barber, and loved ice hockey. He moved to Northern California with his family in 1958, and kept drawing Peanuts until his death in 2000. In 1969, he and his first wife Joyce built an ice rink here, the Redwood Empire Ice Arena, known to everyone as Snoopy's Home Ice. It has a café called the Warm Puppy, and every summer it hosts Snoopy's Senior World Hockey Tournament, with sixty-odd teams of older players from around the world. Schulz was inducted into the U.S. Hockey Hall of Fame in 1983. Just down the street is the Charles M. Schulz Museum, opened in 2002. Its great hall has a 22-foot ceramic mural made of 3,588 Peanuts strips that together form an image of Lucy holding the football for Charlie Brown. And here's a lovely Santa Rosa coincidence. Schulz's first published drawing, in 1937, was a sketch of his family dog Spike, who ate pins, tacks and razor blades. He sent it to Ripley's Believe It or Not, and it ran in the syndicated panel. Robert Ripley, who created Believe It or Not, was born right here in Santa Rosa.

Robert Ripley, born in Santa Rosa in 1890, turned weird facts into an empire. He left high school after his father died, worked as a newspaper sports cartoonist from the age of sixteen, and moved to New York in 1913. In December 1918 he drew his first Believe It or Not! cartoon of strange feats and facts. Readers loved it, and sent in their own oddities: unusually shaped vegetables, strangely marked pets. He took accuracy seriously enough to hire a full-time researcher, a polyglot named Norbert Pearlroth. In 1929 the newspaper magnate William Randolph Hearst syndicated the panel in 360 newspapers and 17 languages, and radio and television shows followed. Ripley also, believe it or not, became the New York State handball champion in 1926. A suitable Santa Rosan for a day full of oddities.

Somewhere beneath this part of Santa Rosa runs one of the most dangerous faults in the Bay Area. The Hayward Fault, which runs under Berkeley, Oakland and Hayward, has a northern counterpart on this side of the bay: the Rodgers Creek Fault, which passes through Santa Rosa. In 2016, researchers showed the two are linked under San Pablo Bay, forming one Hayward-Rodgers Creek Fault about 120 miles long, from north of Heldz-burg to San Jose. Like the San Andreas, it's a right-lateral fault: stand on one side, and the other side slides to your right. It takes up its share of the motion between the Pacific and North American plates. Santa Rosa knows what that means. On the evening of the 1st of October 1969, two earthquakes, magnitude 5.6 and 5.7, struck about an hour and twenty minutes apart, a few miles north of the city on the neighbouring Heldz-burg Fault. Chimneys fell, sidewalks buckled, pipes burst, and one person died; the damage was worse than expected for their size, and modelling suggests the city sits where a sediment-filled basin amplifies the shaking. Because the quakes struck in the evening, few people were out on the streets. The city then set about retrofitting its old brick buildings.
